skill.name: arm-cortex-expert

skill.summary: Build and review ARM Cortex-M firmware with practical driver and safety guidance.

content.value_statement: ARM Cortex-M firmware needs careful driver design, interrupt handling, and hardware validation. This skill provides practical guidance for robust embedded implementations.
actual_capabilities: Designs ARM Cortex-M peripheral drivers for SPI, I2C, UART, ADC, PWM, USB, CAN, and SDIO.
Explains interrupt-safe patterns for ISRs, ring buffers, critical sections, and priority configuration.
Guides DMA and cache coherency decisions for Cortex-M7 devices such as Teensy 4.x and STM32 H7.
Compares platform details across Teensy, STM32, nRF52, and SAMD microcontrollers.
Reviews embedded C, C++, and Rust patterns for memory safety, register access, and deterministic behavior.
Provides debugging checklists for hard faults, stack overflow, timing failures, and peripheral setup issues.
limitations: It cannot verify behavior on real hardware without board access, probes, logs, or test results.
Generated firmware still needs datasheet review, compiler checks, and hardware validation.
It does not replace safety certification, electrical review, or production qualification.
Platform APIs and register names may need adjustment for each vendor SDK version.

use_cases.title: Peripheral Driver Design
use_cases.description: Create a structured driver plan with initialization, interrupts, buffers, and validation steps.

use_cases.title: Board Bring-Up Review
use_cases.description: Check clock setup, pin muxing, voltage assumptions, DMA buffers, and fault risks before testing.

use_cases.title: Rust Embedded Safety Guidance
use_cases.description: Choose safe shared-state patterns for interrupts, atomics, critical sections, and register access.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Driver
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner request for a new peripheral driver.
prompt_templates.prompt: Plan an ARM Cortex-M driver for this peripheral: [peripheral]. Target board: [board]. Include initialization, data flow, error handling, and validation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Review Firmware Design
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this firmware design for [platform]. Focus on interrupt safety, blocking calls, buffer ownership, timing limits, and hardware validation risks.

prompt_templates.title: Debug a Hardware Failure
prompt_templates.prompt: Help debug this Cortex-M issue: [symptoms]. Platform: [MCU]. Include likely causes, registers to inspect, measurements to capture, and safe experiments.

prompt_templates.title: Optimize DMA and Timing
prompt_templates.prompt: Optimize this Cortex-M data path for throughput and deterministic latency. Consider DMA, cache coherency, memory barriers, interrupt priorities, and buffer alignment.

output_examples.input: Design a non-blocking SPI sensor driver for STM32.
output: A driver architecture with initialization, transaction state, chip-select timing, and error paths.
A validation plan covering bus speed, interrupt behavior, sensor identity checks, and timeout handling.

output_examples.input: Review a Teensy 4.x DMA audio buffer plan.
output: A cache coherency review with alignment requirements and memory placement options.
A list of timing risks, interrupt priority checks, and measurement points for hardware testing.

output_examples.input: Explain a hard fault on Cortex-M4 after a peripheral write.
output: A fault triage checklist covering status registers, stack frame inspection, and invalid address checks.
A safe debugging sequence that separates clock, pin mux, pointer, and access-width issues.

best_practices: Provide the exact MCU, board, SDK, peripheral, clock tree, and electrical constraints before asking for implementation help.
Ask for validation steps alongside design output, especially when interrupts, DMA, or hardware timing are involved.
Review generated code against the datasheet, vendor examples, and real hardware measurements before production use.
anti_patterns: Requesting generic firmware without naming the target MCU, SDK, pins, timing needs, or error handling requirements.
Using generated register logic without checking reset values, access widths, volatile behavior, and vendor errata.
Treating simulated reasoning as hardware proof without oscilloscope traces, logs, debugger data, or board tests.

faq.question: What platforms does this skill cover?
faq.answer: It focuses on ARM Cortex-M targets, especially Teensy 4.x, STM32, nRF52, and SAMD boards.

faq.question: Can it write complete firmware?
faq.answer: It can help draft complete modules, but you must compile, test, and adapt them for your board.

faq.question: Does it support Rust embedded development?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers Rust patterns for atomics, critical sections, register access, and interrupt-safe shared state.

faq.question: Can it debug hardware problems?
faq.answer: It can guide debugging with likely causes, register checks, and safe experiments based on your observations.

faq.question: Is it suitable for safety-critical products?
faq.answer: It can support engineering review, but it is not a substitute for certification, formal verification, or qualified expert signoff.

faq.question: What inputs improve the results?
faq.answer: Provide the MCU part number, board, SDK version, peripheral mode, timing limits, pins, logs, and test equipment readings.
